Centroids in Polygon

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: the lines from each corner to the balance point of all the other corners always meet at one dot.
How to play: Drag a corner, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Use the minus and plus buttons for 3 to 20 corners, press Cycle to pick a corner, and tick Hint on a four-corner shape to see why.
4 corners
Look for the math

Drag a corner and the whole picture follows. Yet every line still runs through the same red dot, and that dot always cuts the line in the same fraction. Here is why that cannot fail.

One balance point

Hang a unit weight at each of the N corners. The one point where the polygon balances is the barycenter G = (P1 + P2 + ... + PN) / N: add the corners like arrows and divide by how many there are. That is the red dot in the picture.

The centre of the other corners

Leave one corner out and average the rest. For corner Pi the other N−1 corners have balance point Qi = (sum of all Pj with j not i) / (N−1), marked with a small blue dot. Cycle picks a corner: the green shape joins the other corners, and its green dot is exactly the average of theirs. With four corners, Hint draws the three medians of that trimmed triangle; they cross at the same dot.

Why every line goes through G

Write S for the sum of all the corners. Then Qi = (S − Pi)/(N−1) and G = S/N, so a short calculation gives

Qi − G = −(Pi − G)/(N−1)

The two vectors point in opposite directions along the same line: G lies between Pi and Qi, and PiG / GQi = N−1. This holds for every i at once, so all N lines meet at G. For N = 3 the fraction is 2 to 1, the familiar split of a triangle's medians. The logic test checks all three claims for every N from 3 to 20 on regular, skewed and hundreds of random polygons; none failed.

A smaller copy, turned around

The last equation is one homothety applied to every corner: centre G, coefficient −1/(N−1) = 1/(1−N). So Q is similar to P, just smaller and turned halfway around G; its sides are 1/(N−1) as long and its areas 1/(N−1)² as large. For a triangle this red dot is also the point where the three medians cut the shape into six pieces of equal area. The applet scatters its starting corners with a small random angle; this page fixes that jitter so the first picture is steady. The geometry is the same.

Set four corners, press Cycle and then tick Hint: the green dot is where the triangle's three medians cross, and each median is split 2 to 1 there.
